pinterest.title: Wedding Table Settings, Piece by Piece: Plates, Cutlery, Glasses and Napkins
pinterest.description: How to set a wedding table one place at a time. Cutlery is laid in order of use from the outside in, forks to the left, knives and spoons to the right, the water glass above the knife and wine glasses to its right. Only set what your menu needs, which is why the setting is finalised after the menu. A clear guide to wedding place settings for a plated dinner, a shared table or a long banquet.

pinterest.title: Wedding Table Setting Ideas for Every Theme, from Classic to Coastal
pinterest.description: A theme lives in the finish of each piece, not in adding more. See how the same wedding table setting changes across classic and formal, pared back, garden and romantic, coastal, country estate, winter and candlelit, and playful and retro looks: the plate, the cutlery finish, the glass, the napkin fold and the stationery. Wedding table setting ideas you can take straight to your stylist.

pinterest.title: Wedding Table Settings Abroad: What to Ask Your Venue
pinterest.description: Planning a destination wedding? The tableware a venue holds decides how far a theme can go before pieces need to be hired in. Ask what tableware, glassware and linen it holds, whether it has chargers, who sets and clears the tables, and whether you can see a full mock-up of one place setting before the day. Get the answers in writing before you commit.

slides: Every guest sits down to the same small arrangement. Here is how to set a wedding table, piece by piece.
Start with the menu. Cutlery is laid in the order it will be used, from the outside in, and only what your guests will use is set.
Forks to the left. Knives and spoons to the right, each knife blade facing the plate. Dessert cutlery sits above the plate or arrives with dessert.
The water glass sits above the knife. Wine glasses sit to its right, and at a formal dinner they cascade to the right of the setting.
The napkin goes to the left of the forks or in the centre of the charger. Both are correct, which makes it the easiest place to carry a theme.
A theme lives in the finish of each piece. Heavy white linen and crystal for classic. Stoneware and natural linen for pared back. A knotted napkin and sea glass for coastal.
Marrying abroad? Ask the venue what tableware it holds, what must be hired in, and ask to see a mock-up of one place setting.
Tell us the look you love and where you are marrying. Send us a message and a Wedded Advisor will talk your reception through with you.
instagram_carousel.caption:
A wedding table is built one place at a time. Before the florals arrive and the candles are lit, every guest sits down to the same plate, cutlery, glass, napkin and name card, and that arrangement tells them how the evening will run.

Our new guide works through each piece in the order it is laid: cutlery from the outside in, forks to the left, knives and spoons to the right, glasses above the knife. Then it shows how classic, pared back, garden, coastal, country estate, winter and playful themes change the same pieces, through the finish rather than by adding more.

Planning a wedding abroad? The guide also sets out what to ask your venue about tableware, glassware and linen before you fall for a look it cannot lay.

Which theme is closest to your table? Tell us in the comments, or send us a message to talk it through with a Wedded Advisor. Full guide at the link in our bio.
